message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and federal law. Keep in mind that local rules can add extra protections, so it’s always a good idea to check your city or county regulations as well. | Category | What You’re Entitled To | Practical Tips | |----------|------------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Get a written receipt for the deposit.
• Request a written itemized list of deductions if you receive a partial refund. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• Must comply with all applicable building, health, and safety codes. | • Document any problems (photos, written notice).
• If the landlord fails to fix major issues, you may withhold rent or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct remedy. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord does not fix a major problem within a reasonable time after notice, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent (up to the amount of the rent). | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much a landlord can raise rent, but they must give **at least 30 days’ written notice** before the increase takes effect. | • Review your lease for any specific notice period; if it’s longer than 30 days, that applies. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month** tenants: Landlord must give **30 days’ written notice** to terminate.
• Tenants must give **30 days’ written notice** to terminate a month‑to‑month lease. | • Provide notice in writing (email or certified mail) and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the formal eviction procedure (notice, court filing, judgment).
• Common grounds: non‑payment of rent, violation of lease terms, or unlawful activity. | • If you receive an eviction notice, respond promptly. Seek legal counsel or tenant advocacy groups. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Protected under the **Fair Housing Act** and Texas’ own anti‑discrimination laws. Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • Report discrimination to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Health & Safety** | • Landlord must maintain smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors, and fire extinguishers. | • Test detectors regularly; report failures immediately. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide essential utilities (water, heat, electricity) unless otherwise specified in the lease. | • Verify utility responsibilities in your lease. | | **Tenant’s Right to Repair** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent (up to the amount of the rent). | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Legal Assistance** | • Texas has several tenant advocacy organizations and legal aid services that can help with disputes, evictions, and lease negotiations. | • Contact local legal aid or tenant unions for free or low‑cost advice. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – Look for clauses about security deposits, maintenance responsibilities, notice periods, and any “no‑fault” clauses that might waive your rights. 2. **Ask for a written itemized list** of any existing damages or repairs needed before you move in. 3. **Confirm the landlord’s obligations** regarding utilities, repairs, and habitability. 4. **Verify the notice period** required for both you and the landlord to terminate the lease. 5. **Check local ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas, Houston) have additional tenant protections such as rent control or stricter eviction procedures. --- #### When Things Go Wrong | Issue | Your Options | How to Proceed | |-------|--------------|----------------| | Landlord refuses to make necessary repairs | • File a complaint with the local housing department.
• Consider withholding rent or repairing and deducting. | • Document the problem and send a written notice. | | Unlawful eviction notice | • Respond in writing.
• Seek legal assistance or contact HUD. | • File a counter‑claim in court if necessary. | | Discrimination claim | • File a complaint with HUD or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | • Gather evidence (emails, witnesses). | | Security deposit dispute | • Request an itemized deduction list.
• File a claim in small claims court if unresolved. | • Keep receipts and correspondence. | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a habitable home, timely notice for rent increases or termination, protection against discrimination, and the ability to withhold rent or repair‑and‑deduct if the landlord fails to maintain the property. Always keep written records, communicate in writing, and know your local ordinances for extra safeguards. If you encounter a problem, consider reaching out to a local tenant advocacy group or legal aid service for guidance.
